A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GTM defense. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison. The original appendices are retained, with the qualitative-results appendix moving from F to G to accommodate new analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original masking experiments, defense success rates, utility and computational measurements, ablations, and qualitative results in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds high-resolution recognition, adaptive-attack, and practical token-alignment evaluations in Appendix F.

M1.justification: GTM's hidden-state gradient saliency, top-k token selection, masking and response-generation procedure remain unchanged in Section 4 and Algorithm 1. The 5% masking ratio is also retained. Appendix F evaluates the existing defense under additional conditions.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds HR-Bench-4K, requiring recognition of tiny objects in high-resolution images, and a stronger threat scenario involving attackers explicitly adapted to GTM. UltraBreak also expands jailbreak coverage. JPS and AdvBench were already present; using the full AdvBench evaluation set is a protocol addition.

E2.justification: The new JPS comparison in Table 12 includes first-token logit-based masking, which was absent from v1's JPS comparison in Table 9. Logit attribution already appeared separately in Table 6. Existing comparator membership in Tables 1–9 is retained.

E3.justification: New adaptive evaluations introduce saliency regularization, defense-in-the-loop optimization and differentiable soft masking. Strategies 1–2 use 1,000 steps and bounds of 32/256 and 64/256, with strongest-ASR selection across regularization coefficients; soft masking is attempted for 10,000 steps. Appendix F.3 adds full-AdvBench evaluation on Qwen2-VL-7B. These are additional protocols; existing experiments retain their stated settings.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds substantial tests of three previously unexamined questions: whether masking harms tiny-object recognition disproportionately, whether defense-aware attackers circumvent GTM, and whether the attribution advantage extends to practical token-alignment attacks. Existing masking ablations, sliding-window analyses and DiffPure failure cases remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. v2's multiple trials over the regularization coefficient constitute parameter search, without introducing repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 10–12 add HR-Bench-4K accuracy of 61.75% versus 67.62% undefended; adaptive ASRs of 4.55%/19.09% at 32/256 and 26.36%/31.82% at 64/256; and GTM ASRs of 7.88% on UltraBreak and 20.19% on JPS. Soft masking reportedly fails to optimize successfully. Original results are retained, including Table 9's separate JPS result; the new full-AdvBench evaluation does not establish a same-setting performance change.

T1.justification: Appendix F.2 newly defines the top-k saliency regularizer and its combined cross-entropy attack objective. Existing token-alignment assumptions, saliency definition, ranking statements and Appendix B proofs are unchanged. Main-text theorem renumbering and Equation 6's equality notation do not introduce a new guarantee; that equality already appeared in v1's appendix.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about sparse adversarial dependence, hidden-state attribution, ranking consistency, low overhead and effective defense with preserved utility. The added appendix evidence does not revise these central claims.

C2.justification: Appendix F substantially expands applicability and mechanism discussions. It distinguishes spatially sparse benign objects from concentrated adversarial dependencies, acknowledges increased vulnerability under adaptive attacks while claiming partial protection, and explains soft-mask optimization instability. It also argues that textual steering and prefix injection make token alignment practically relevant.

D1.justification: The added analyses document image resolution, evaluation scope, adaptive loss construction, masking during optimization, perturbation bounds and iteration budgets. Exact regularization sweep values and soft-mask parameters are unspecified. Existing hardware information and the code-access statement remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Cui et al. (2026) for UltraBreak and Wang et al. (2025b) for the high-resolution benchmark, connecting the added analyses to recent work. The related-work narrative remains substantially unchanged. VMA's citation suffix changing from 2025b to 2025c identifies the same work.

P1.justification: v2 inserts Appendix F and relabels the existing qualitative appendix as G. Other edits include removing one author affiliation, correcting main-text theorem numbering and a corollary reference, reducing repeated citations, and fixing limited spacing and spelling issues. Most original prose and organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds three compact result tables, numbered 10–12. The original qualitative table becomes Table 13 and follows the new analyses. Existing figures and table designs are retained, with limited repositioning and page reflow.

improvement.justification: Appendix F provides useful scrutiny absent from v1, particularly adaptive attacks exposing ASR up to 31.82%, a 5.87-point HR-Bench utility loss, and practical attribution comparisons. These additions clarify empirical limits. The improvement remains limited by incomplete adaptive-attack specifications and insufficient integration of the qualifications into the main text, which still describes utility degradation as virtually absent.
